chunks: And regarding the foot, when it breaks and is set without deformity or defect, is one-fifth of the wergild of the leg, being two hundred Dinars; and the wergild of its exposure is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and regarding the displacement of its bones is one hundred Dinars, half the wergild of breaking it; and regarding a piercing in it which does not close, is one-fifth of the wergild of the leg, being two hundred Dinars; and regarding a bruising in it is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being fifty Dinars.

key_terms.نَافِذَة: A piercing or hole that does not close

ai.seo_question: What is the financial compensation for a broken foot in Shia Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi provides a precise jurisprudential breakdown of *diyah* (blood money) for foot injuries, distinguishing between fractures, bone displacement, and specific defects like exposed or non-healing wounds. It reflects the Shia scholarly tradition of quantifying compensation based on the severity and permanence of the injury, using the Dinars as a standard currency of the time. The detailed categorization underscores the legal rigor applied to bodily integrity in Islamic inheritance and tort law.
